hints: Look carefully at the right-hand end of the graph where substrate concentration is very high. Do the dashed (with inhibitor) and solid (without inhibitor) curves reach the same plateau or different plateaus?

Remember that plateau height is Vmax, and Km is the substrate concentration needed to reach half Vmax. Think about how a competitive inhibitor fighting for the active site changes the substrate needed to get to half speed.
walkthrough:
**Read what the graph is telling you**

Look at the two curves. At low substrate, the dashed line is lower. But at very high substrate concentration, the dashed line catches up and reaches the same flat top as the solid line.

That flat top is $V_{max}$, so $V_{max}$ is unchanged.

**Recall what Vmax and Km mean**

$V_{max}$ is the maximum rate when every active site is filled with substrate.

$K_m$ is the substrate concentration needed to reach half of $V_{max}$. A higher $K_m$ means lower affinity, you need more substrate to get to half speed.

**Apply competitive inhibition logic**

A competitive inhibitor binds reversibly to the active site, so it blocks substrate at first. If you add lots more substrate, the substrate outcompetes the inhibitor and fills all sites.

That is why $V_{max}$ can still be reached, but you need more substrate to get to half $V_{max}$, so $K_m$ increases.

options.A: Both parts are wrong. The graph shows the same plateau, so Vmax does not decrease, and more substrate is needed for half speed, so Km does not decrease.
options.B: Vmax staying the same is correct, but Km decreasing is backwards. A decreased Km would mean higher affinity, while a competitive inhibitor lowers apparent affinity.
options.C: This matches the graph and theory. High substrate outcompetes the inhibitor so Vmax stays the same, but more substrate is needed to reach half Vmax so Km increases.
options.D: This describes non-competitive inhibition, not competitive. A non-competitive inhibitor lowers Vmax with Km unchanged, but here Vmax is unchanged.
